CausalChain: HCC tumor cells overexpress PD-L1 -> PD-L1 engages PD-1 on T cells, suppressing anti-tumor immunity -> Oncolytic viruses preferentially infect HCC cells and induce immunogenic cell death -> Engineered oncolytic viruses (with tumor-selective promoters and safety switches) deliver AI-optimized CRISPR/Cas9 components targeting PD-L1 -> Targeted CRISPR-mediated PD-L1 disruption reduces immune suppression -> Reduced PD-L1 levels enhance T cell activation -> Synergistic use with immune checkpoint inhibitors leads to robust anti-tumor response and tumor regression
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that oncolytic viral vectors, enhanced with tumor-selective promoters and integrated safety mechanisms and equipped with AI-optimized CRISPR/Cas9 systems targeting the PD-L1 gene, can effectively and safely disrupt PD-L1 expression in hepatocellular carcinoma cells. This targeted gene editing will alleviate tumor-mediated immune suppression and, when combined with immune checkpoint inhibitors, will produce a synergistic anti-tumor response that overcomes tumor heterogeneity and leads to significant tumor regression.
Abstract: We propose an integrated therapeutic strategy for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) that leverages an advanced oncolytic viral platform engineered to deliver CRISPR/Cas9 components specifically targeting the PD-L1 gene. By incorporating tumor-selective promoters (e.g., AFP promoter) and built-in safety switches, the vector is designed to achieve high-fidelity, cell-specific gene editing while minimizing off-target effects. Enhanced with contemporary technologies such as AI-optimized guide RNA selection, real-time viral tracking, and multi-modal imaging, this approach aims to robustly disrupt PD-L1 expression in tumor cells. The resultant reduction in local immune suppression is expected to synergize with immune checkpoint inhibitor therapy, thereby augmenting T cell-mediated anti-tumor responses and promoting tumor regression. Our strategy builds on existing evidence of effective CRISPR/Cas9-mediated PD-L1 disruption via adenoviral vectors while addressing key challenges such as specificity, safety, and tumor heterogeneity in HCC.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed the use of oncolytic viral vectors engineered to deliver CRISPR/Cas9 for PD-L1 gene disruption in HCC cells, combined with checkpoint inhibitors for a synergistic effect. The revised hypothesis retains this core concept but enhances it by explicitly incorporating elements to improve specificity and safety: (1) The addition of tumor-selective promoters (e.g., AFP promoter) ensures that the viral vector selectively infects HCC cells, addressing concerns about off-target editing. (2) Integrated safety switches ameliorate risks associated with CRISPR/Cas9 delivery. (3) The use of AI-based optimization for guide RNA design and real-time imaging technology further improves the efficiency and tracking of the vector, thus tackling issues of heterogeneity and delivery variability. These enhancements address the weaknesses noted in the review while maintaining the original causal chain and overall strategy.
